#4610. Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

#4609. Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 11:16 AM EST

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your new favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered issue, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

So when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

The options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.)

The solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

Harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

These days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

The idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.)

In the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to New York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

His wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It took Stockard’s death, a new boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

#4608. Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 new cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she said.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang said those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang said that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang said she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The New England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang said she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”

#4607. Thanksgiving Outside the Echo Chamber

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

“Polarized” has been one of the most overused words to describe America's political climate, but it is increasingly being applied to school boards, neighborhoods, and even families as well. Affective polarization, or the growing dislike and distrust of people on the opposing side of the political aisle, has more than doubled in the U.S. since the late 1970s (Boxell et al., 2024). Many of us now surround ourselves with like-minded friends and partners, creating a world in which we watch news, follow influencers, and make friends with people who reinforce what we already believe. This all gets thrown out the window at Thanksgiving, when we leave the safety of our echo chamber and spend time with the family we didn’t choose but love anyway.

Historically, the weird uncle at the Thanksgiving table could be counted on to tell a few off-color jokes or ask a child to pull his finger. These offenses seem almost quaint now that a passing comment about politics or social justice can leave half the table questioning the moral character of the other half. This annual exercise ends in one of two ways: The dinner crescendos into an actual altercation with one side accusing the other of crimes against humanity, or everyone smiles politely, and then unloads their thoughts and feelings to their significant other on the ride home. I’d like to propose a third option: intellectual curiosity.

What if we approached a conversation with someone whose political beliefs we find baffling with a genuine interest in how they came to hold those beliefs in the first place? It is true that not all beliefs are equal (beliefs such as racial superiority are indefensible); however, many people come to believe something they consider logical based on their life experience. For example: free college for all. Imagine cutting into the turkey when one family member casually says free college could open doors for students whose families can’t afford an education, and another relative pipes up that that wouldn’t be fair. Eating slows, as everyone recognizes dinner just got awkward.

Rather than writing off the relative you disagree with, use this time to practice intellectual curiosity, or the desire to learn, explore new ideas, and better understand something, even when it challenges what we already believe. This requires a couple of steps. The first is to pause. Polarizing comments are often triggering, and people often get angry before anything else. Recognize the anger and then pause until the initial rush passes.

Next, commit to intellectual curiosity by asking instead of telling. In the free college example, this may mean replying with, “I’d like to hear more about that. What feels unfair to you?” And then sit back and actually listen. Make eye contact, don’t interrupt, and don’t prepare your next argument. Doing this requires the next step: using your Theory of Mind.

Theory of Mind is the ability to understand that others have thoughts, beliefs, desires, and intentions that differ from our own. Because we can’t open someone’s head and look inside, we don’t know what they're actually thinking, but we gather clues from what they say and how they act to develop a theory of their mind. Theory of Mind develops rapidly across childhood and adolescence and continues into adulthood. This doesn’t mean all adults are good at it; in fact, I’d argue that most aren’t. We're already using Theory of Mind when we judge our relatives. We're just doing it with very little information and potentially a great deal of bias. When someone opposes free college, we might immediately assume they're selfish or indifferent to disadvantaged students. That assumption is itself a theory of their mind. Asking questions allows us to gather better information and revise that theory. At the Thanksgiving table, this means trying to put yourself in their shoes and take their perspective.

Finally, we can muster empathy. We’ve asked questions, revised our theory of their mind (why they believe what they do), and we still disagree with them. That’s okay; we can hold our beliefs and still find space in our heart to empathize with theirs. To return to the free college debate, imagine that a relative shares that they had to graduate in 5 years rather than 4 because they worked two jobs to pay for their education. Despite this, it still took them 17 years and a lot of low-budget vacations to pay off their loans, a milestone they just recently celebrated. Suddenly the word “fair” hits differently. You empathize with their situation, although you may still retain your initial position.

By the end of the night, you may still find your uncle’s political beliefs baffling, but you’ll better understand how he came to hold them. Given how much time we spend speculating about the minds of people we disagree with, why not take advantage of having one sitting across the table from us? Ask a few questions, entertain the possibility that you’ve misjudged someone, and see where the conversation goes. You might even have a more pleasant ride home.

Boxell, L., Gentzkow, M., & Shapiro, J. M. (2024). Cross-country trends in affective polarization. The Review of Economics and Statistics, 106(2), 557–565. doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_01160

Premack, D., & Woodruff, G. (1978). Does the chimpanzee have a theory of mind? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1(4), 515–526. doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X00076512

Stanley, M. L., Sinclair, A. H., & Seli, P. (2020). Intellectual humility and perceptions of political opponents. Journal of Personality, 88(6), 1196–1216. doi.org/10.1111/jopy.12566

#4606. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4605. Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 12:05 PM EST

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took issue with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered new approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”

“I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup said in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”

It took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”

Instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen said this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

“This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

But does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” said Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”

Okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he said. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”

#4604. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4603. Why Stress Is Good for You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The old story about stress is that you wanted to avoid it wherever possible, and you especially wanted to avoid responding to stressors if you could. You wanted to be calm, untroubled, and chill most of the time.

This old story has been found to be absurdly, wildly wrong, but still it persists like a bad dream, while those of us who respond powerfully to life's ups and downs have been taught to question ourselves constantly (and then stress out about our stress responses).

The new story may surprise you, because it focuses on the strengthening power of stressors, the health benefits of a strong stress response, and the cognitive interventions that can help you access the healing heart of stress.

First things first. Stress is not a thing that happens to you; it's a deeply individual response to something that matters to you.

An alternative definition for the word stress is to underscore, highlight, or focus on something because it's important to you. Your stress responses are connected to how much importance you place on a potential stressor. The higher your stress response, the more importance the stressor has for you.

If your stress response is high, you're not failing at being chill, and the stressor didn't make you react; you're marking something as deeply important and worthy of your focus and attention. So the first intervention is to focus on what's important to you

In her book The Upside of Stress: Why Stress is Good for You and How to Get Good at It, researcher Kelly McGonigal focuses on a research-backed group of simple mindset interventions that help people reframe their relationship with their stress responses.

Instead of trying to get you to calm down, McGonigal helps you identify and then write about the values that are most important to you. This might seem to be a strange approach, but the connection between importance and your stress response is very clear. As such, connecting to your values can help you identify and then learn about the things that mean the most to you.

With these interventions, your stress responses can help you develop deep knowledge about who you are and what's important to you. And perhaps, instead of seeing yourself as a stressed-out mess, you can reframe yourself as a person who feels deeply and cares deeply.

If you've been exposed to any form of stress management, mindfulness, or meditation that pathologizes your stress responses, you need to read The Upside of Stress and support yourself with healthier ideas.

In part 2 of this series, I focused on a surprising and heartening aspect of our newer knowledge about stress: The strength of your stress response is not a problem at all, because it's directly connected to your resilience and your skills.

You may have heard the saying, "Teach your butterflies to fly in formation." This comes from people like actors, athletes, skydivers, and other professionals who choose to be in stressful situations as a part of their livelihoods. Research has shown that high-performing people don't develop lower stress responses over time; they stay high. But what changes over time is their relationship to their stress responses.

Instead of fretting or trying to manage, suppress, or downregulate their stress responses, high-performing people learn to reframe their heightened activation as necessary for preparation and mastery. Many even learn to see their robust stress responses as zest for life.

This is true even for people like skydivers, whose work (or play) is literally life-endangering. Their stress responses are valuable forms of activation that prepare them for uncertainty (and fun).

Learning to reframe your stress responses means learning how to support your necessary activation as you face uncertainty. Stress is good for you.

In part 1 of this series, I focused on the "weasel word" of stress, which hides the true, emotional nature of our stress responses from us. Unmasking our emotions and learning how to identify and work with the energy and focus they bring to us means that we can develop robust skills for times when the chips are down, and our deepest values are engaged.

Researcher Lisa Feldman Barrett (and colleagues) have shown that simply identifying and naming our emotions with precision can help us develop strong emotion regulation skills—with no other intervention. So, if we persist in misidentifying our emotions with the weasel word of stress, we can't develop those skills.

In part 1, I identified the three powerful emotions that are usually a part of our stress response (anxiety, panic, and anger), and I offered some ideas for how to work with them intentionally. My book, The Language of Emotions, focuses on how we can learn to access the astonishing genius in all of our emotions.

Another old story about stress is that our brains react to the world: A stressor "happens," and our brains and bodies react without thought or choice. But researchers have understood for decades that our brains are predicting the future instead of reacting like hapless jack-in-the-boxes.

This predictive nature means that our brains are using our stores of past knowledge to help us make predictions and decisions about what may happen next.

If we believe outdated and damaging information about our stress responses, that bad information will become a self-perpetuating part of our predictions, and we'll misread our activation as a problem instead of a necessary part of preparation, resilience, and mastery.

When we have better information about stress, the values we hold, the importance of our strong stress responses, and the emotional truth hidden inside the weasel word of stress, we can reframe stress as necessary. And we can set ourselves up for better predictions in the future.

McGonigal, K. (2016). The Upside of Stress: Why Stress Is Good for You, and How to Get Good at It. New York, NY: Avery.

McLaren, K. (2023). The Language of Emotions: What Your Feelings Are Trying to Tell You. New York, NY: St. Martin's Essentials.

#4602. First albatross egg of the season spotted at Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 2:03 PM EST

Nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

One special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

#4601. Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Learn the basics to keeping your heart healthy

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

“Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

“Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he said that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”

An AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

“Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”

Other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen said.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

“Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen said.

“Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

Still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”

#4600. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4599. South Korea will use emergency alert system to warn about exam cheaters

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:10 PM EST

On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

The aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

The sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student said in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place new anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be new concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

#4598. Farewell Concentration Camp Ballerina

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Dr. Edith Eva Eger, sometimes called the female Viktor Frankl, died this year at age 98. At age 16, Edith and her family were deported to Auschwitz. She and her mother stood in line before the Angel of Death, Dr. Josef Mengele. Mengele directed the mother to go toward the gas chamber, and pointed Edith in a different direction to live. As Edith watched the smoke rise from the gas chamber, she knew her separation from her mother was permanent. That night, Mengele forced Edith, a gymnast and ballerina, to dance for him. In the depths of her numbness and grief, she willed herself to dance, then kindly shared the bread that Mengele disdainfully tossed her with other prisoners.

In facing this experience and other childhood adversities, Edith showed remarkable courage and resilience. Her mother was critical, being stuck in grief and anger for losing her mother as a child. Edith felt like the invisible sister, only gaining a sense of worth when she was able to rescue her parents from their loneliness and pain. She was cruelly shamed for being Jewish and teased for her awkwardness and crossed eyes. She coped with her sense of shame by becoming a perfectionist in gymnastics and dance to gain approval.

In overcoming her pain, she learned wisdom that she shared well into her 90s as a practicing psychologist. For example, she taught of the peace of having a clear conscience, relating that Mengele would always have to live with what he’d done; he was more of a prisoner than she was.

Edith taught that one survives adversity by committing to a cause outside of self and focusing on what one still has. In the concentration camp, she participated in mock beauty pageants and fantasized about a delightful future and a loving marriage. Although the circumstances were depressing, she realized that she had a purpose and that only she could do certain things in the way that she could.

Rather than becoming embittered, she clung to her faith, reasoning that it wasn’t God who ran the death camps, but hateful people. Even among the Germans, she found people who were secretly kind. She experienced, and chose to believe, that imperfect people are redeemable. She even forgave her German captors, whom she believed were themselves prisoners.

Understandably, Edith suffered long after her liberation. Yet she came to believe that suffering can reveal inner strengths and grow the confidence that one can endure intense adversity. She chose to believe in hope, love, and her ability to find joy in nature and little children.

She also encouraged people to tell their story in safe and appropriate ways, to release pain’s grip. She courageously accepted an invitation to return to Germany, where Hitler had once stood, and returned to Auschwitz to come to peace with her haunting memories.

Edith showed us how to overcome crushing adversity by reclaiming one’s sense of worth and purpose. In her healing journey, she gained hard-earned wisdom that she generously shared with others, still high-kicking into her 90s.

Her life reminds us that suffering crosses everyone’s path. That suffering can be a stumbling block or a stepping stone to greater resilience and life satisfaction (Schiraldi, 2021; 2017). We thank her for her inspiring example. Rest in peace, Edith Eva Eger.

Eger, E. E. (2017). The Choice. New York: Scribner.

Schiraldi, G. R. (2021). The Adverse Childhood Experiences Recovery Workbook. Oakland, CA: New Harbinger.

Schiraldi, G. R. (2017). The Resilience Workbook: Essential Skills to Recover from Stress, Trauma, and Adversity. Oakland, CA: New Harbinger.

#4597. Huawei set to challenge Tesla Powerwall with new, 20 kW home battery

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That’s enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you’ll want to keep going if you’re preparing for more than a day or two without power.

If that sounds like you, Luterra’s got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel.

Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

Nice, but no mention of price or European availability.

Alas, the Luterra S2 probably won’t be making its way to the US anytime soon – but fear not! If you’re shopping for a Tesla Powerwall alternative that won’t help fund the absolute worst people in politics, there are a number of great home battery systems on the market that can deliver backup power, store your solar energy, and keep your home running when the grid goes down. #4596. Fiona the hippo under 24-hour care after swallowing hat

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:54 PM EST

UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”
